newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Central bankers want safety nets dismantled - BIS.
newsitem.headline: Central bankers want safety nets dismantled - BIS.

text.p: With inflation subdued and growth looking promising, central bankers are turning their attention to overall financial stability and urging governments to tear down safety nets and let weak banking institutions fail.

As suggested by recent financial shocks, central banks have made more headway in establishing monetary stability and buoyant growth than in creating financial stability, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Monday.

Lasting financial stability, however, might not be achieved unless a better balance was struck between authorities and market players, BIS president and chairman Wim Duisenberg told the bank's 67th annual meeting. This was a task that required broad political commitment and went beyond the realm of central banks.

Despite the benign economic outlook, BIS said in its annual report, there were still short-term risks, including U.S. inflation, a weak Japanese financial sector, vulnerable European market sentiment and remarkably buoyant financial markets.

"Perhaps the most pressing concern is that inflationary pressures in the United States may prove more difficult to tame than is now anticipated and the expansion may eventually end abruptly," Duisenberg said. This could lead to tightening with significant impact on stock prices and other more risky financial instruments.

"The question is whether the macroeconomic risks have been correctly valued and factored into asset prices or whether the materialisation of any of them could trigger some broader form of retrenchment," Duisenberg said.
BIS, the bank to the world's central banks, took the same questioning line on whether risks had been properly assessed.
"If not, the search for higher yields...could easily turn into a widespread search for enhanced protection should bad news emerge from whatever source," it said in its report.

Financial and monetary stability were closely related and the challenge for central bankers was to find mechanisms that safeguarded both objectives amidst continuing deregulation, technological change and innovation, BIS said.
Cooperation among financial market supervisors had to be improved across geographical and institutional borders. Public dislosure also had to be improved and regulation made more market-friendly.

Financial institutions had to be better managed, BIS said, recalling that trading losses at major firms had gone undetected for years. This showed the deficiency of many internal risk management systems. "Nevertheless, individual and market discipline cannot ultimately be effective if agents act on the expectation of insulation from losses in the event of distress," said Duisenberg.

"At the very least, reconciling prudential safeguards with this philosophy (of free markets) calls for a reduction in the compass of the overly generous safety-net arrangements that, de jure and especially de facto, have operated for so long in a number of segments of the financial industry."
"Dealing with these issues is a task that clearly goes well beyond the remit of prudential supervisors and central banks," he said.

The headway made in monetary policy in recent years is largely due to the growing political and social consensus over the merits of price stability and the willingness of governments to give central banks a mandate for price stability.

"In the short term, industrial countries inflation is expected to remain generally subdued and growth, on balance, to strengthen, as those economies less advanced in the cycle catch up," Duisenberg said.
"Similarly, the overall growth and inflation prospects in the non-industrial world are very positive," he added.
The only problem with a continuing low inflation was people might forget the cost of inflation and once again seek to push demand beyond sustainable limits.
But just as it would be premature to declare inflation dead, BIS cautioned it would be unwise to assume that sound economic fundamentals guaranteed good performance.
Perhaps the most pressing concern, BIS said, was that inflationary pressures in the United States might prove more difficult to tame and the expansion might eventually end abruptly.
This could have a significant impact on stock prices and other more risky financial instruments.

Other sources of risk to the global economy stemmed from the need for structural reform in Europe and turbulence in the run- up to a single European currency along with continuing weakness in the Japanese financial sector.
In Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe the challenge was to restore competitiveness without inflation picking up.
"The fact that banking systems in many of these countries are quite fragile is clearly another source of uncertainty about the macroeconomic outlook," BIS added.
